audience: Introductory; IT, facilities, procurement and sustainability colleagues with basic data-center familiarity

modules.title: Why Liquid Cooling Now?
outcomes: Explain when rising heat density creates a cooling constraint.
Trace heat from a component through transport to final rejection.
Distinguish cold plates and immersion independently of single-phase and two-phase operation.
Separate heat capture, facility efficiency, water use and heat reuse.

slides.title: Why Liquid Cooling Now?
slides.narration_intent: Introduce the practical question: how do we remove heat from the equipment a site needs to deploy? Promise a usable vocabulary and a way to ask informed questions. Keep the opening self-contained and welcoming.
slides.visual: Module title with simple course mark. No year or upgrade badge.

slides.title: Four Decisions Along the Cooling Path
slides.narration_intent: Preview the four modules in their original order. Explain that this is an introduction for facilities, IT, procurement and sustainability colleagues. No engineering calculations or specialist prerequisite course is required. Set an approximately one-hour learner expectation.
slides.visual: Four-module course roadmap.

slides.title: Heat Density Changes the Cooling Question
slides.narration_intent: Connect processor heat concentration, rack load and deployment conditions. Explain why a high total rack load and a difficult local hotspot are related but different problems. Air cooling remains appropriate for some loads; an equipment requirement or site limit can make liquid necessary. Avoid a universal transition threshold.
slides.visual: Qualitative component and rack sketches; no unsupported density cutoff.

slides.title: Follow the Heat All the Way Out
slides.narration_intent: Build the shared mental model: acquire heat, transport it, then reject or beneficially reuse it. Follow one load through each stage. A cold plate or tank does not make heat disappear. The final facility cooling path still needs capacity, whether heat reaches it through water or air.
slides.visual: Silent short-loop schematic: component to coolant to heat exchanger to facility rejection. Heat pulses cross the exchanger; separate fluids never mix.

slides.title: Cooling Method and Fluid Phase Are Separate Choices
slides.narration_intent: Use two independent questions. Where is heat acquired: at a cold plate or from immersed equipment? Does the working fluid remain liquid or boil and condense? Show all four combinations without suggesting that every fluid, component or design can be exchanged between them. Define dielectric in context.
slides.visual: Two-by-two matrix with cold plate and immersion as rows and single-phase and two-phase as columns.

slides.title: Air and Liquid Often Share the Work
slides.narration_intent: Explain targeted cold-plate heat capture, remaining air-cooled components and rear-door heat exchangers. A rear door transfers heat from rack exhaust air to liquid; it is a different acquisition point from a cold plate. A highly liquid-cooled tray does not automatically make a complete rack or building air-free.
slides.visual: Heat-path comparison with a visible residual-air branch. Mark boundaries explicitly.

slides.title: Choose for the Workload and the Site
slides.narration_intent: Organize the adoption decision around equipment requirements, facility capacity, operational readiness and business need. Compare a dense accelerator addition with a general-purpose server refresh. The question is which supported cooling path fits each case, not which method always wins.
slides.visual: Two short site scenarios with qualitative requirement cards.

slides.title: Measure Benefits at the Right Boundary
slides.narration_intent: Define power usage effectiveness as facility energy divided by IT energy over a consistent period. Separate that ratio from liquid heat-capture percentage and useful computing output. Energy, water and heat-reuse results depend on the complete installation, load and conditions. Replace universal savings promises with a measured baseline.
slides.visual: Boundary diagram and a compact metric comparison, without numerical savings claims.

slides.title: Find the Right OCP Cooling Community
slides.narration_intent: Introduce Cooling Environments as the top-level OCP project. Locate cold plates, CDUs, immersion, door heat exchangers and heat reuse. Explain that open interfaces and shared qualification make a system easier to evaluate; a published specification is not proof that any two products are compatible.
slides.visual: Five-area project map and one live Cooling Environments project link.

slides.title: Keep the Complete Heat Path in View
slides.narration_intent: Recap why heat density matters, the acquisition-transport-rejection path, the independent architecture and phase choices, and the need to measure at a defined boundary. Ask the learner to name one missing facility question before selecting hardware.
slides.visual: Four concise takeaways.

slides.title: Check the Cooling Mental Model
slides.narration_intent: Orient the learner to one single-answer question and one multi-select question. Ask them to distinguish architecture from phase and identify the missing system responsibilities. Explain that both questions need an attempt; feedback and retry support learning and correctness is not required to continue.
slides.visual: Two-question knowledge check with instructional feedback.

slides.title: Next Explore Direct Liquid Cooling
slides.narration_intent: Acknowledge completion of module one. Explain that the next module follows a cold-plate loop and examines the interfaces that keep it reliable. Direct the learner to module two through the LMS module list.
slides.visual: Module-complete page and LMS navigation instruction.

questions.prompt: A coolant boils inside a cold plate attached to a processor. Which description fits?
choices: Two-phase direct liquid cooling
Two-phase immersion cooling
Single-phase immersion cooling
Rear-door air cooling only
questions.feedback: Phase change describes fluid behavior. Cold plates identify the heat-acquisition architecture; boiling does not make a cold-plate design immersion.

questions.prompt: Which statements support a sound cooling decision? Select all that apply.
choices: Identify the complete heat-rejection path
Check the workload and site requirements
Use a defined boundary when comparing efficiency claims
Assume all liquid-cooled racks need no airflow
questions.feedback: A supported decision connects the load, the full heat path and the measurement boundary. Residual air-cooled loads may remain.

modules.title: Direct Liquid Cooling (DLC)
outcomes: Identify the main components in a cold-plate cooling path.
Distinguish a technology loop from the facility side of a heat exchanger.
Explain the introductory roles of fluid qualification and connector compatibility.
Recognize the different facility paths illustrated by Deschutes and Brazos.

slides.title: Direct Liquid Cooling
slides.narration_intent: Introduce a contained coolant path that collects heat through cold plates. Set the outcome: identify the complete loop and the evidence needed at its interfaces. Define DLC again so the module can be taken independently.
slides.visual: Module title and cold-plate mark.

slides.title: Trace the Loop and Review Its Interfaces
slides.narration_intent: Preview cold plates, manifolds, hoses, connectors and the coolant distribution unit. Establish the four review questions: where heat goes, which fluid is approved, how parts connect and who maintains the system.
slides.visual: Four objectives tied to a simple loop silhouette.

slides.title: Cold Plates Collect Heat at Its Source
slides.narration_intent: Trace coolant from supply through a qualified connector and cold plate to return. Explain conduction from the component to the plate and heat transfer into fluid. Identify the manifold as distribution rather than a heat-rejection device. The animation illustrates single-phase DLC; other cold-plate loops can use phase change.
slides.visual: Silent short-loop diagram of supply, manifold, cold plate and return. Leave the facility boundary visible.

slides.title: A CDU Connects Two Cooling Responsibilities
slides.narration_intent: Define the technology cooling system and facility water system. Show a typical liquid-to-liquid CDU transferring heat across an exchanger while keeping its fluids separate. Pumps, sensors and controls support the selected design. Use Deschutes as a named example and route detailed sizing and controls to its live course.
slides.visual: Two-loop diagram with a heat-exchanger boundary and visible Deschutes course pill.

slides.title: Select a Qualified Fluid for the Actual Loop
slides.narration_intent: Replace the false water-versus-glycol dichotomy: a water-glycol mixture is water-based. Explain heat transport, freeze protection, additives, cleanliness and wetted-material compatibility at a beginner level. PG25 is a defined propylene-glycol mixture, not a guarantee against microbes or a maintenance-free label. Introduce dielectric fluids for some two-phase designs without treating them as interchangeable with immersion fluids.
slides.visual: Fluid-family tree and supplier-evidence checklist. Links to the live fluids and two-phase DLC courses.

slides.title: Liquid Cooled IT Can Reject Heat to Facility Air
slides.narration_intent: Compare the previous liquid-to-liquid path with a liquid-to-air sidecar. Introduce Project Brazos as a current retrofit example: its local loop receives IT heat and its exchanger returns that heat to facility air. Existing air handling still removes the load. Sufficient power, airflow, temperature margin and capacity remain essential.
slides.visual: Side-by-side paths; Brazos is one example, with its live course link. Omit chassis counts, ratings and control details.

slides.title: A Quick Disconnect Is a Defined Interface
slides.narration_intent: Define quick disconnect and distinguish hand mating from blind mating. Introduce universal quick disconnects and MGX Quick Disconnects as different named families. MQD and MQDB now have a published OCP companion specification. Teach matching family, size, revision, mating method, coolant and application. Never imply that a shared label alone establishes cross-vendor or cross-family compatibility.
slides.visual: Generic connector-interface cards and location map. Link MGX module 5 through the live course page; no dimensional drawing or assumed cross-mating.

slides.title: Reliability Depends on the Whole Wetted System
slides.narration_intent: Connect fluid chemistry with metals, polymers, seals and cleanliness. Explain why leakage, blocked flow and contamination need different evidence and responses. Startup records, sampling, filtration condition, leak detection and maintenance ownership support reliability. More flow or replacing fluid without root-cause analysis is not a universal remedy.
slides.visual: Risk-to-evidence map for leak, flow restriction and chemistry.

slides.title: Review a Cold Plate Retrofit Proposal
slides.narration_intent: Present a liquid-cooled server proposal for an air-cooled room. Ask what is missing if it lists cold plates and a coolant name but no final heat-rejection capacity, connector revision or operating owner. Identify a possible Brazos-type path without prescribing it. Require qualified thermal and hydraulic evidence before deployment.
slides.visual: Scenario annotation; reveal missing handoffs after reflection.

slides.title: Treat the Loop as an Integrated System
slides.narration_intent: Recap cold plates, heat-exchanger boundaries, qualified fluids, specified connectors and the remaining facility duty. Emphasize that a well-performing component cannot establish the reliability of the assembled system.
slides.visual: Four concise system takeaways.

slides.title: Check the Loop and Compatibility Decisions
slides.narration_intent: Explain that the questions ask where heat goes in a liquid-to-air retrofit and which evidence supports a compatible fluid connection. Give the same attempt, feedback and retry instructions as module one without reading the answer choices.
slides.visual: Two-question knowledge check.

slides.title: Next Examine Immersion Cooling
slides.narration_intent: Acknowledge completion of the DLC module. Preview the change in module three: hardware is immersed in qualified dielectric fluid, with different equipment, service and heat-rejection requirements. Use the LMS module list to continue.
slides.visual: Module-complete page with module three title.

questions.prompt: A Brazos-type liquid-to-air sidecar removes heat from a server coolant loop. Where does that heat go next?
choices: Into facility air that still needs to be cooled
It disappears inside the sidecar
It necessarily enters facility chilled water directly
It becomes a reduction in the IT electrical load
questions.feedback: The exchanger transfers heat to facility air. The building still needs enough heat-removal capacity for that load.

questions.prompt: What evidence belongs in a quick-disconnect compatibility review? Select all that apply.
choices: Specified family size revision and mating method
Coolant and wetted-material compatibility
Applicable operating and qualification evidence
A shared marketing label is sufficient
questions.feedback: Compatibility is defined by the actual mating interface, fluid, conditions and qualification. A label or similar appearance is insufficient.

modules.title: Immersion Cooling Essentials
outcomes: Explain single-phase and two-phase immersion without confusing them with two-phase DLC.
Trace the bath heat path beyond the tank.
Identify equipment, materials, warranty and service evidence needed for adoption.
Compare potential benefits with facility and fluid lifecycle obligations.

slides.title: Immersion Cooling Essentials
slides.narration_intent: Introduce immersion as a system designed around equipment in dielectric liquid. Frame the module around how heat moves, what hardware qualification means and how service work changes. Avoid presenting immersion as universally better than cold plates or air.
slides.visual: Module title with generic tank mark.

slides.title: Evaluate the Tank and the Installation
slides.narration_intent: Preview the two phase modes and the practical adoption questions. Explain that nonconductive fluid supports the intended electrical environment, while equipment qualification, safety controls and procedures remain necessary.
slides.visual: Four learning objectives.

slides.title: Single Phase Immersion Keeps the Bath Liquid
slides.narration_intent: Follow heat from immersed components into dielectric liquid and through the selected circulation and heat-exchange path. Show that circulation may be designed around forced flow or natural convection. The bath remains liquid. Remove the original implication that a simple label guarantees lower maintenance or a particular flow requirement.
slides.visual: Silent short-loop tank schematic showing warm fluid, heat exchange and cooled return.

slides.title: Two Phase Immersion Boils and Condenses
slides.narration_intent: Follow boiling at hot surfaces, vapor movement, condensation and liquid return. The operating fluid and containment system are selected for that cycle. Contrast this bath arrangement with phase change inside cold plates: both use latent heat, but their equipment and fluid circuits differ. Avoid numerical boiling or environmental claims.
slides.visual: Second silent short-loop schematic, with liquid and vapor paths visually distinct and a condenser boundary.

slides.title: The Tank Still Needs a Complete Heat Rejection Path
slides.narration_intent: Connect the bath or condenser to its external cooling path and eventual heat rejection or reuse. Discuss the physical footprint, filled weight, service access and supporting plant. Immersion may remove server fan duty but does not abolish pumps, exchangers or building heat-removal responsibilities.
slides.visual: Tank-to-facility boundary diagram; no blanket HVAC-elimination claim.

slides.title: Qualify Equipment Fluid and Service Together
slides.narration_intent: Explain why boards, cables, connectors, seals and labels need compatibility with the actual fluid and operating conditions. Service includes safe lifting, draining, handling, cleaning and controlled return to operation under approved procedures. Do not treat an air-cooled server as immersion-ready simply because it fits in the tank.
slides.visual: Equipment-fluid-process qualification triangle and service sequence.

slides.title: Obtain Written Warranty and Safety Evidence
slides.narration_intent: Separate a fluid test, a component evaluation, a system safety assessment and a commercial warranty. Ask who covers the actual server, tank and fluid combination, under which conditions, and who owns a failure investigation. OCP guidance and independent safety programs support evaluation; neither provides a universal warranty.
slides.visual: Four evidence cards and a written-coverage question.

slides.title: Evaluate Benefits Against the Installation
slides.narration_intent: Discuss possible reductions in server fan energy and noise, and potential heat-reuse opportunities. Compare those opportunities with pumping, heat rejection, space, maintenance and fluid stewardship. Water use depends on the final cooling method. Assess the selected fluid using current supplier, environmental and end-of-life evidence rather than a blanket claim about all two-phase fluids.
slides.visual: Benefit-and-obligation comparison with explicit facility and lifecycle boundaries.

slides.title: Ask Whether an Immersion Pilot Is Ready
slides.narration_intent: Present a pilot with an attractive efficiency claim but no documented equipment coverage, lifting process or heat-rejection plan. Ask the learner to identify the missing evidence. Emphasize a supported trial with clear acceptance criteria and ownership; a low claimed PUE is not a readiness decision.
slides.visual: Pilot-readiness scenario with evidence gaps. Optional live immersion track link.

slides.title: Immersion Readiness Extends Beyond the Bath
slides.narration_intent: Recap the two phase modes, the continuing facility heat path and qualification of equipment, fluid and service together. Keep warranties and lifecycle records specific to the selected installation.
slides.visual: Four concise takeaways.

slides.title: Check Phase Change and Adoption Readiness
slides.narration_intent: Orient the learner to the single-phase versus two-phase distinction and the evidence needed before a pilot. Repeat that both questions require a submit attempt, feedback explains the reasoning and retry is available.
slides.visual: Two-question knowledge check.

slides.title: Next Plan Deployment and Operations
slides.narration_intent: Acknowledge completion of immersion essentials. Explain that the final module joins architecture choices to site readiness, commissioning, operating ownership and measurable value. Continue through the LMS module list.
slides.visual: Module-complete page and module four title.

choices: Bath fluid boils at hot components and vapor condenses back to liquid
The bath stays liquid while only its temperature changes
Only coolant in processor cold plates changes phase
Every facility heat-rejection component is removed
questions.feedback: Two-phase immersion uses boiling and condensation in the immersion arrangement. It still needs a supported condenser and downstream heat path.

questions.prompt: Which evidence should an immersion pilot review include? Select all that apply.
choices: Compatibility of the actual equipment and fluid combination
Written warranty coverage and responsibilities
Service handling and facility heat-rejection readiness
A low claimed PUE replaces equipment qualification
questions.feedback: Pilot readiness combines equipment, fluid, commercial coverage, service and facility evidence. An efficiency claim does not replace any of them.

modules.title: Operations, Planning & Strategic Value
outcomes: Outline site, vendor and operating responsibilities before a deployment.
Explain why commissioning must test complete handoffs and fault responses.
Distinguish energy, water, heat reuse and fluid lifecycle evidence.
Select a relevant live Academy course or OCP community for further learning.

slides.title: Operations Planning and Strategic Value
slides.narration_intent: Introduce the shared task of turning a cooling option into a supported operating system. Set the outcome: ask for the site, vendor, commissioning and lifecycle evidence needed for a responsible decision.
slides.visual: Module title and installation mark.

slides.title: Make a Supported Deployment Decision
slides.narration_intent: Preview site readiness, clear ownership, integrated commissioning, monitoring and evidence of value. State that the course supports informed collaboration; detailed design and operating procedures come from the qualified installation and its responsible teams.
slides.visual: Four objectives with a deployment-review diagram.

slides.title: Check the Site Before Ordering Equipment
slides.narration_intent: Review the complete path: available electrical and heat-removal capacity, temperatures, routing, load and floor constraints, containment, access and service space. Apply the same questions to cold plates, a Brazos-type retrofit and immersion. A rack position or compatible connector alone does not prove site readiness.
slides.visual: Site plan with heat path, access and service boundaries.

slides.title: Assign Each Interface and Failure to an Owner
slides.narration_intent: Connect IT, facilities, cooling integrators, fluid suppliers and operations. Procurement needs approved interfaces, compatibility evidence, warranty terms, spares, training and escalation routes. Show how a gap between suppliers becomes an operating risk. Do not imply that cross-team coordination is unique to liquid cooling.
slides.visual: Responsibility table for equipment, loop, facility path and operating response.

slides.title: Commission the Handoffs Before Accepting the System
slides.narration_intent: Show a high-level sequence from installation checks to approved cleaning and fill, baseline sampling, load testing, fault-response evidence and operating handover. Describe the purpose of each stage without prescribing chemistry, pressures or a universal sequence. A component factory test does not establish complete installation performance.
slides.visual: Silent short-loop animation of evidence handoffs; all stages complete before acceptance.

slides.title: Turn Monitoring Signals Into an Agreed Response
slides.narration_intent: Relate temperature, flow, pressure, leak alarms and fluid-quality trends to system condition. Explain why operators need baselines, thresholds, escalation and recovery procedures agreed with responsible suppliers. An alarm is evidence to interpret, not a diagnosis by itself. Do not recommend generic dosing or pump-speed changes.
slides.visual: Signal-to-question-to-owner flow with three example observations.

slides.title: Build the Business Case Across the Lifecycle
slides.narration_intent: Compare capital work, operating energy, service effort, supply continuity, equipment utilization and downtime exposure. Keep energy, water and carbon boundaries explicit. Heat reuse requires suitable heat, a useful demand, an interface and a viable arrangement. Fluid recovery or disposal must follow the actual fluid and qualified service pathway.
slides.visual: Lifecycle decision table; no guaranteed payback, emissions reduction or recyclability.

slides.title: Review One Proposal With Four Evidence Questions
slides.narration_intent: Return to the common scenario of adding liquid-cooled compute at an existing site. Ask whether the complete heat path is supported, interfaces and materials are qualified, operations and failure responses have owners, and the claimed value has a measured basis. Missing evidence calls for a supported next step rather than an automatic yes or no.
slides.visual: Capstone decision card; compare air-side retrofit, facility-water integration and immersion at a qualitative level.

slides.title: Continue With the Course That Matches Your Question
slides.narration_intent: Route coolant chemistry and operations to the fluids course, facility-water CDUs to Deschutes, liquid-to-air retrofit to Brazos, connector integration to MGX and Open Rack, phase-change cold plates to two-phase DLC, and architecture tradeoffs to Thermal Boundaries. Point community participation to Cooling Environments and its Summit track. These are optional follow-ons.
slides.visual: Clickable learning map. Keep titles and descriptions brief; link each destination once on the slide.

slides.title: Ask for Evidence From Component to Facility
slides.narration_intent: Summarize the complete course: match cooling to the workload and site, qualify interfaces and fluids, assign operational ownership and measure actual value. Encourage one practical next action: bring these questions to a deployment review.
slides.visual: Course-wide takeaways, followed by the final module check.

slides.title: Check Deployment Judgment
slides.narration_intent: Explain that the questions test readiness and the evidence supporting a sustainability claim. Both questions need an attempt; feedback and retry are available. Avoid trivia about a generic cooling-energy percentage or unsupported supplier guarantees.
slides.visual: Two-question knowledge check.

slides.title: Apply the Cooling Review Questions
slides.narration_intent: Thank the learner for completing module four and encourage them to use the review questions with their team. Direct them to the LMS to confirm all four module completions and to the continuing-learning resources. Do not infer overall course completion merely because this page was reached.
slides.visual: Final-module completion page with centered live catalog and Cooling Environments links. Preserve original contributor credits in written credits without implying endorsement of the update.

Assume a published connector specification covers the site

Assume liquid cooling guarantees lower carbon and water use at every site
